newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: URGENT MEETING ON BUY-OUT OF PNG MINE
In Melbourne today, the Bourgainville Copper Limited Board will hold an urgent meeting about the P-N-G government's announcement it wants to buy-out majority shareholder RTZ-CRA.
The PNG government has moved to reduce the price it may have to pay to buy out RTZ-CRA's 53 per cent interest in the Bougainville Copper Mine.
Although no official offer has been made, there are suggestions the company could be billed for the Bougainville war.
Sources close to PNG Prime Minister, Sir Julius Chan claim the government will take the position that the war on Bougainville was the fault of the RTZ-CRA.
It's claimed any purchase price would have to take into account the costs run up by the Government since the insurrection began.
YOUNG DOCTORS REP TO MEET WITH NSW CABINET
In New South Wales, a young doctors' representative will brief state Cabinet in Tamworth today on their Medicare provider number dispute with the Commonwealth.
Medical officers in New South Wales are taking indefinite industrial action over Federal government restrictions on doctors entering general practice.
NSW Health Minister, Andrew Refshauge, says Cabinet is keen to hear first hand the concerns of young doctors about their career prospects.
CYCLONE JUSTIN ONE OF THE LARGEST IN YEARS
The weather bureau says Tropical Cyclone Justin is one of the largest low pressure systems seen for years.
Forecaster, Jeff Crane says the category two cyclone is more than one-thousand kilometres wide, and remaining almost stationary in the Coral Sea.
He says Justin's expected to stay within a tight circle for most of the day before moving towards the coast tonight or tomorrow.
Cyclone Justin is now 620 kilometres east of Cairns and 520 kilometres northeast of Bowen.
CONFERENCE ON PORT ARTHUR MASSACRE IN MELBOURNE
A two-day conference examining the aftermath of the Port Arthur massacre begins in Melbourne today.
Speakers will discuss police, ambulance and hospital response as well as the effects on the local community the eeconomic impact and media management.
It's hoped the conference will provide information to disaster response groups throughout Australia.
Speakers will include Tasmanian Police Commissioner, Richard Mcreadie.
TEACHERS DISGUSTED WITH MINISTERS HANDLING OF REPORT
In Sydney's west, staff at Mt Druitt High School say they're angry and disgusted with the way the Education minister has handled a report into the performance of senior students.
Education minister John Aquilina yesterday released a review of last year's HSC class, which recorded the worst marks in the state.
In a letter to Mr Aquilina, teachers criticised the leaking of the report to a Sydney newspaper the previous day and the paper's use of a photograph identifying the students.
The staff claim they were not informed of the release of the report or given a copy before its public release and say they've been betrayed by the minister.
At a stopwork meeting yesterday, Mt Druitt teachers pass a motion of no-confidence in Mr Aquilina and have demanded a meeting with him.
MOUNT KOSCIUSKO'S NAME MAY CHANGE
What's in a name?
A lot according to the Geographical Names Board.
It says the name of Mount Kosciusko should be changed so that a "z" is included after the last "s" in the word.
That was the spelling of Tadeusz Kosciouszko, after whom the Australian landmark was named.
The Geographical Names Board has pondered public submissions on the matter.
It's told New South Wales Land Minister Kim Yeadon a "z" should be used in all future correspondence, mentioning Mount Kosciusko.
And the Executive director of the committee lobbying for the change, Chrisitna Landis, says the pronunciation of the mountain's name should be changed accordingly.
CABINET CONSIDERS WORK-FOR-DOLE SCHEME
The Federal Opposition says it won't block the Government's planned work-for-the-dole pilot scheme for young unemployed people, which Cabinet will consider today.
The Government plans to introduce legislation into Parliament next week to change social security and industrial laws so the 15-million dollar scheme can be made compulsory for some.
The Vocational Education and Training minister, David Kemp, will put to Cabinet a one-year plan, for up to 70 work-for-the-dole projects involving 10-thousand unemployed 18 to 24 year olds.
The first projects are due to start in September, run by local government, welfare agencies and service groups, in areas of high unemployment, with emphasis on the regions.
COLLECTABLE CAR AUCTION IN MELBOURNE
An auction of collectable cars in Melbourne has raised nearly two million dollars.
Shannons Auctioneers held the special auction as part of the Grand Prix celebrations, and say the sale was a great success.
Ninety Seven vehicles went under the hammer, with the top money earner a 1915 Locomobile Speedster, going under the hammer for 180-thousand dollars.
Shannon's spokesman Michael Browning says the Speedster would probably realise up to double that on the world market in good times.
He says it cost ten times the purchase price of a Model T Ford when new, and is a unique vehicle.
MELBOURNE'S AIR QUALITY IMPROVES
The Environment Protection Authority says there's been a steady improvement in Melbourne's air quality, but there's no room for complacency.
Only four smog days have been declared this summer, compared to 24 during Melbourne's last scorching summer of 1982-83.
EPA Chairman, Dr Brian Robinson says tighter industry regulations, an end to backyard burning and motor vehicle and diesel emission standards have all contributed.
He says public transport is important to air quality, since cars are the dominant factor in air pollution.
Dr Robinson says a coming development will be so-called telecommuting, where many more people will be able to work from home via their computer links.
